"I think I always throw myself in these impossible situations and then see if I can scramble out of them and gain something from these experiences," he told CNN during rehearsals for the December performances. "Standing in front of the orchestra was intimidating at times, but I think we got through it, and I think we made some exciting waves in town. We definitely got the crowd excited about it." Leehom has certainly made waves with his Mandarin-language pop music, having sold around 15 million records, but as his recent foray in classical music confirms, he's more than just another voice with an interesting haircut. Growing up in the U.S. to a family of doctors, he excelled at school but decided to take a different path to his parents. After shunning the opportunity to study at an Ivy League university, he spent some time at Williams College of liberal arts before getting his big break in pop in Taiwan in 1995. At that time he admits he knew nothing about Chinese music and didn't speak Mandarin. Learning Mandarin was just another challenge Leehom rose to meet and he believes that having Chinese as a second language has been to his advantage, and his interest in the linguistics of the language has led to some of his more innovative work. "I always think for artists to take their shortcomings and turn them around and make them into what define them as an artist is a real trick," he told CNN. "I think it's a wonderful thing for people to understand how language can be transformed and mutilated for musical reasons and actually bring out something special orally," he said. Musically he's often been put in the same box as Mando-pop sensation Jay Chou, and has similarly has been the subject of rumor about ever aspect of his life, from his school grades to his sexuality.  Watch Wang Leehom talk about his rivalry with Jay Chou ». Adding his face to a number of endorsements, the pressures of being in the public eye have made him become increasingly protective of his privacy. "It's definitely changed me. It's like some defense mechanism I guess, to just be private, to keep things to myself, to protect myself or my loved ones. I am the same person, but just a different way of life," he said. However it hasn't stopped him from branching out and taking on an acting career. He made his big screen debut in 2000 in the Hong Kong action flick "China Strike", but it was his role in Ang Lee's international success "Lust, Caution" that brought him wider international attention. As for taking on new projects in the future, be they film, singing or even holding the baton once again, Leehom will stay true to his policy of challenging himself with different ventures. "Sometimes it gives me a lot of trouble, sometimes it ends up launching a career which has been very good for me," he said.

Despite the controversies, Wang Leehom’s influence on Mandopop remains significant. For many fans, he represents a generation of artists who helped internationalize Chinese pop music — bringing together American musical training, Mandarin songwriting and a polished global pop sensibility.

From a U.S. upbringing to Asian superstardom, Wang’s career reflects the complicated demands of modern celebrity: artistic reinvention, commercial visibility, cultural translation and the constant pressure of life in the public eye.

**Leehom Wang on Rehearsing With the Hong Kong Philharmonic, Career Choices, and the Long Road Back to the Music**

*By [Reporter Name]*  
*Hong Kong — [Date]*

The rehearsal room is quieter than expected until the first swell of strings arrives. Cellos enter warmly, violins answer in a bright arc, and a familiar melody—one that many Mandarin-pop listeners know by heart—takes on a new shape in the hands of the Hong Kong Philharmonic Orchestra.

At the center of it stands Leehom Wang, listening intently.

He is not performing yet. He is watching the conductor, following the brass, checking the balance between the orchestra and the rhythm section. Every few bars, he leans forward, makes a note, then looks back up as if hearing a song from his own past being returned to him in a different language.

“Pop music is often built in layers,” Wang says during a break in rehearsal. “But with an orchestra, the layers breathe. You can’t force it. You have to respect the space between the notes.”

Wang’s collaboration with the Hong Kong Philharmonic marks a significant artistic moment for the singer-songwriter, producer, actor, and multi-instrumentalist, whose career has long moved between classical training, R&B, hip-hop, Chinese traditional elements, and Mandarin pop. For an artist who built his reputation on crossing musical borders, the orchestral setting feels less like reinvention than a return to first principles.

“I started with violin,” he says. “So when I hear a symphonic arrangement, it feels very close to my roots. At the same time, these songs carry so many memories for listeners. The challenge is to honor that, but also give them a new emotional dimension.”

## “Every Choice Costs Something”

Wang’s career has rarely followed the safest route. Born in Rochester, New York, and later educated at Williams College and Berklee College of Music, he entered the Mandarin-language music industry as a bilingual, bicultural artist at a time when the market was still defining what “global Chinese pop” could sound like.

His early success positioned him as a polished balladeer, but he soon pushed toward more ambitious fusions: Western R&B grooves, Chinese opera textures, hip-hop production, erhu and pipa colors, and lyrics that often moved between romance, identity, and cultural pride.

Looking back, Wang says many of his choices were driven by curiosity rather than calculation.

“I don’t think I was ever good at staying in one lane,” he says with a laugh. “Sometimes that helped me. Sometimes it confused people. But every choice costs something. If you try to make new sounds, some listeners may need time. If you repeat yourself, you may lose yourself.”

He pauses before adding: “The important thing is knowing why you’re doing it.”

That question—why—has followed Wang throughout his decades in the industry. He became one of Mandopop’s most recognizable stars, known for his musicianship, clean-cut image, and wide appeal across Taiwan, mainland China, Hong Kong, Southeast Asia, and overseas Chinese communities. His work helped shape the idea that Mandarin-language music could be both commercially powerful and musically hybrid.

Yet fame also created expectations.

“When people see you through songs, screens, interviews, headlines, they form a version of you,” he says. “That version may be partly true, but it is never complete.”

## On Mandarin Music and Cultural Confidence

Ask Wang about the state of Mandarin-language music today, and he becomes animated. He speaks less like a veteran guarding his legacy than a student eager to compare notes with a new generation.

“The most exciting thing now is that Mandarin music is no longer looking for permission,” he says. “Young artists are making music that is local and international at the same time. They are not asking, ‘Can this travel?’ They already assume it can.”

For Wang, who spent much of his career discussing cultural identity through music, that shift feels meaningful.

“In the early days, there was often this question: How do we combine East and West?” he says. “But maybe the next generation doesn’t need to phrase it that way. Their lives are already mixed. Their playlists are mixed. Their languages are mixed. So the music comes out naturally.”

Still, he believes language remains central.

“Mandarin has its own rhythm, its own emotional weight,” he says. “A melody changes when you put Mandarin lyrics on it. The tones, the vowels, the way certain words land—it’s not just translation. It’s composition.”

That sensitivity to language is part of what has made songs like “Kiss Goodbye,” “Forever Love,” “The One and Only,” and “Change Me” endure. In orchestral rehearsal, those melodies sound expansive but still intimate, reminding listeners that Wang’s catalog has always depended not only on production but on melodic clarity.

“A good song should survive many arrangements,” he says. “If it only works because of one beat or one sound, maybe it is not finished yet.”

## The Weight of Public Image

Wang has also lived through the more difficult side of celebrity: scrutiny, controversy, and the collapse of a carefully maintained public image. He does not dwell on specifics in this conversation, but he acknowledges that public perception can change quickly and painfully.

“There are things you can explain, and things you have to live through,” he says. “I’ve learned that image is fragile. Music has to be stronger than image.”

He says the past few years have changed how he thinks about performance.

“When you are younger, you may think the goal is to be understood,” Wang reflects. “Later, you realize that being understood by everyone is impossible. So the work becomes: Can I be honest? Can I be responsible? Can I keep improving?”

Does he feel nervous returning to major stages?

“Of course,” he says. “If you don’t feel anything, that means you don’t care. But nerves can be useful. They remind you that the moment matters.”

During rehearsal, that seriousness is visible. Wang repeatedly asks to run transitions again, especially where the orchestra moves from lush cinematic passages into more rhythm-driven sections. He pays close attention to tempo, dynamics, and phrasing.

“This kind of collaboration requires humility,” he says. “You are not bigger than the orchestra. You are inside it.”

## On Jay Chou and the Idea of Rivalry

No conversation about Wang’s generation of Mandopop is complete without mentioning Jay Chou. For years, fans and media framed the two as rivals: both male singer-songwriters, both influential, both associated with expanding the sound of Mandarin pop in the 2000s.

Wang smiles when the comparison comes up.

“I understand why people like comparisons,” he says. “It gives them a story. But music is not a race with one finish line.”

He is careful and respectful when speaking about Chou.

“Jay has his own universe,” Wang says. “That is what great artists do—they create a world that belongs to them. I have always respected that.”

Did the rivalry narrative ever affect him?

“If you are honest, of course you are aware of it,” he says. “Awards, charts, headlines—those things are part of the industry. But if you spend too much time looking sideways, you stop moving forward.”

He adds: “Competition can push you, but comparison can trap you. I think we all contributed something different to Mandarin music.”

## Returning to the Stage

The upcoming performance with the Hong Kong Philharmonic is not merely a greatest-hits presentation, Wang says. It is an attempt to reinterpret the emotional architecture of his work.

“There are songs I wrote when I was a very different person,” he says. “When I sing them now, I’m not trying to pretend I’m that same person. I’m singing them with everything that has happened since.”

That gives older material new tension. Love songs become less innocent, anthems more reflective, and familiar choruses carry the gravity of time.

The orchestra, too, changes the relationship between performer and audience.

“In a pop concert, the energy often comes from volume, lights, movement,” Wang says. “With an orchestra, the power can come from restraint. One oboe line can break your heart. A quiet string entrance can say more than a huge beat.”

He hopes audiences will hear both the scale and vulnerability of the arrangements.

“I want people to feel that these songs have grown up with them,” he says.

## Future Projects

As for what comes next, Wang says he is working on new music, though he avoids giving a firm release date. He hints at material that continues his interest in blending genres while sounding “more direct” emotionally.

“I’m writing,” he says. “Some songs are still searching for their final form. I don’t want to rush them.”

He is also interested in more cross-disciplinary projects, including film scoring, orchestral collaborations, and possibly mentoring younger musicians.

“I’ve learned a lot through mistakes and through time,” he says. “If that can be useful to younger artists, I’d be happy to share it.”

Would he consider a large-scale world tour again?

“If the music is ready and the audience is ready, yes,” he says. “But I don’t want to do things only because they are expected. I want the next chapter to have meaning.”

## “The Music Remembers”

Near the end of rehearsal, the orchestra returns to a familiar ballad. This time, the arrangement begins almost transparently: a few strings, a piano figure, Wang’s voice entering gently above them. The room seems to hold its breath.

For a few minutes, the noise surrounding celebrity—the debates, comparisons, disappointments, nostalgia, and reinvention—falls away. What remains is melody, discipline, and the strange durability of songs written years ago that still find new rooms to inhabit.

Wang listens to the final chord fade.

“That’s the beautiful thing,” he says quietly. “People change. The industry changes. Your life changes. But the music remembers.”

Then the conductor raises his baton again, and they start from the top.
